title: Technology Acceptance, Task-Technology Fit, and Perceived Productivity among Microsoft 365 Users  in Bangladesh
content: This study examines how technology-acceptance perceptions and task-technology alignment relate to perceived productivity among Microsoft 365 users in Bangladesh. The research addresses a context-specific gap: evidence on productivity within integrated digital-work ecosystems in Bangladesh remains comparatively limited, while the practical value of such suites depends not only on whether users find the technology useful but also on whether it fits the tasks they perform. A total of 385 complete responses were analysed. The instrument contains three-item measures of perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), task-technology fit (TTF), and task efficiency/productivity (PROD). Composite-score structural analysis was conducted alongside reliability, convergent-validity, discriminant-validity, collinearity, descriptive, subgroup, and mediation diagnostics. PEOU positively predicted PU (standardized β=0.224, p<.001), while TTF also predicted PU (β=0.276, p<.001). Productivity was positively associated with PEOU (β=0.243, p<.001), PU (β=0.151, p=.003), and TTF (β=0.212, p<.001), with R²=0.219. The indirect PEOU→PU→PROD effect was positive (bootstrap 95% CI 0.009 to 0.063). Cronbach’s alpha was below conventional thresholds for all four constructs, requiring cautious interpretation and indicating a need for further scale refinement. The study contributes a dual-route productivity explanation-acceptance/usefulness and task fit-while treating AI-feature experience as contextual information rather than as an undocumented causal construct.
